strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: joint, end-to-end generation of mixed-type covariates, event times, and censoring indicators for survival data, where the only prior tailored method (SurvivalGAN) uses a staged GAN pipeline.

The proposed survival-tailored Cox loss with sparsity-aware exponential weighting for late/rare events is a sensible design choice that is well-motivated by the risk-set instability problem in partial likelihood estimation under censoring.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: three real clinical datasets with varying censoring rates, three families of evaluation metrics (covariate fidelity, downstream C-index/Brier score, and dedicated survival fidelity metrics such as RMST gap and KM MSE), five downstream survival models, and 10 seeds per configuration.
Additional robustness checks such as downsampled dataset experiments and training-loss convergence plots (Appendix E, F) support the claim of stable end-to-end optimization.

Hyperparameters and baseline settings are documented in detail (Appendix A/B), aiding reproducibility, and the method is grounded in established diffusion (VE-SDE, masked diffusion) and survival (Cox partial likelihood) theory.
weaknesses: The empirical superiority narrative is inconsistent with the actual numbers: e.g., TVAE outperforms SurvDiff on Wasserstein distance for GBSG2 and is competitive on METABRIC (Table 2); TabDiff outperforms SurvDiff on Brier score for METABRIC and on RMST gap/KM MSE in Table 7. These contradictions to the "consistently outperforms" claim in the abstract/text are not adequately discussed or reconciled.

The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the diffusion backbone (forward/reverse processes, architecture) is directly borrowed from TabDiff, and the main new ingredient is a Cox loss with a heuristic exponential decay weighting scheme (threshold τ, decay rate α) whose selection and sensitivity are never ablated or justified quantitatively.

No proper ablation isolating the individual contributions of (a) the survival loss itself, (b) the sparsity-aware weighting, and (c) the adaptive λ_surv calibration scheme; the paper only compares against a naive TabDiff baseline, which conflates all these design choices at once.

Evaluation is restricted to three small, classic survival datasets (686–1903 patients), all low-dimensional; scalability to larger or higher-dimensional clinical datasets, and computational cost relative to baselines, is not discussed.

No direct metric evaluates preservation of the censoring mechanism itself (e.g., comparing marginal censoring rates or censoring-time distributions between synthetic and real data); claims about "faithfully preserving censoring" rely indirectly on KM curves and downstream metrics.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests) is reported despite overlapping standard deviations in several comparisons, making some of the claimed improvements difficult to assess as robust rather than noise.

No code/repository link is provided for reproducibility beyond hyperparameter tables, and it is unclear whether SurvivalGAN and other baselines were retuned specifically for the datasets used versus reused as-is from prior work.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: existing tabular diffusion models are not designed to jointly capture censoring mechanisms and time-to-event structure, and the only prior tailored method (SurvivalGAN) is GAN-based with known staged/error-propagation issues.

The proposed survival-tailored loss (Cox partial likelihood integrated into the diffusion training with sparsity-aware exponential decay weighting for late/rare events) is a sensible and reasonably novel design choice that is well motivated by the small-risk-set instability problem in censored data.

The adaptive scaling scheme for balancing the diffusion loss and survival loss (calibrated so the survival term contributes a target fraction of the total objective) is a practical engineering contribution that plausibly improves training stability across datasets with very different loss scales.

Empirical evaluation spans three real clinical datasets (AIDS, GBSG2, METABRIC) with differing censoring rates, and the paper reports both covariate fidelity (JS/Wasserstein distance) and downstream utility (C-index, Brier score) across five different downstream survival models, giving a fairly broad view of performance.

Additional experiments (t-SNE visualizations, Kaplan-Meier comparisons, training loss curves, and a downsampling sensitivity study) support the central claims and show the method is not brittle to smaller sample sizes, which is practically relevant in medical settings.

The paper is clearly structured, provides an extensive appendix with hyperparameters for all baselines (matching prior published settings for fairness), improving transparency and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of "preserving the censoring mechanism" is not convincingly substantiated: the method appears to generate the event indicator E via masked diffusion on the observed label jointly with covariates, but the paper explicitly notes that "administrative censoring can be applied post hoc," which suggests the actual censoring-generating process (which is often informative/covariate-dependent in practice) is not modeled with any tailored mechanism beyond fitting the marginal/joint distribution the diffusion model already targets. There is no experiment that specifically probes whether SurvDiff captures dependent/informative censoring versus just approximating the joint empirical distribution.

Results are less consistent than the text suggests: in Table 2 SurvDiff is not best on Wasserstein distance for METABRIC (TVAE and TabDiff are competitive or better), and in Table 7 (survival metrics) TabDiff or SurvivalGAN outperform SurvDiff on RMST gap and KM MSE for AIDS and METABRIC. Statements like "consistently outperforms" overstate the actual pattern of mixed results, and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across seeds) is reported to support superiority claims.

The ablation supporting the core motivating claim of the paper (that naive application of a tabular diffusion model like TabDiff fails to capture survival structure, motivating the added survival loss) is only indirectly shown through the main comparison tables; there's no controlled ablation isolating the incremental effect of the survival loss/sparsity weighting alone (e.g., SurvDiff without Lsurv, or without the sparsity-aware weights) to verify these specific design choices are responsible for the reported gains rather than architectural/training differences.

The datasets used are relatively small and few (686–1903 patients across three datasets); no larger-scale or more heterogeneous clinical datasets (e.g., with more covariates, competing risks, or truly informative censoring) are used to test generalizability, limiting the strength of the significance claims.

The Cox-based survival loss inherits a proportional hazards assumption; the paper does not discuss how this assumption might bias generated event-time distributions when the true underlying process is non-proportional, which is an important and unaddressed limitation for a paper claiming to "faithfully reproduce the event-time distribution."

No discussion of privacy risks or re-identification concerns despite the explicit motivation of enabling data sharing/accessibility for patient-level clinical data — an ethical dimension that is standard to address in synthetic health-data papers but is entirely absent here.

No code/repository link is provided for reproducibility, despite detailed hyperparameter tables; combined with the complexity of the joint masked+Gaussian diffusion architecture and calibration procedure, independent reproduction would require considerable re-implementation effort.
